periods.analysis: We opened the arc in green: Average Customer Service Response Time was 3.3 hours against the <=4 hour target, and Service Requests Closed Within SLA was 91.4% against the >=90% target. That is a solid operating margin, not a mystery; Dispatch Team B kept the Bayfront, North Hill, and Marina routes clean in Cityworks, and the after-hours utility phone tree was checked daily instead of when somebody remembered. The pipes are still pipes, so the call mix included leak checks, meter-box lids, and pressure complaints, but the customer side did not become the bottleneck. This quarter gives us a useful baseline for defending staffing and software asks with evidence rather than adjectives.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green by keeping the 7:30 a.m. triage huddle and the same-day assignment rule for leak, no-water, and sewer-odor tickets. Extend the Cityworks closeout audit to a weekly 25-ticket sample by route, with Utilities Crew Leads signing off on missed SLA causes. Use the 3.3 hours and 91.4% baseline in the FY2025 budget file to justify maintaining dispatcher coverage during summer peak demand.

periods.analysis: We stayed green, but the shape changed: response time moved up from 3.3 hours to 3.9 hours quarter over quarter, while SLA closure improved from 91.4% to 92.1%. That tells me the front door slowed a bit during the holiday leave and first coastal storm cycle, but once requests were assigned, crews closed work more consistently. South Harbor meter route M-17 and pressure-zone calls around PRV-4 added volume, and the two-person customer service desk absorbed it without losing the SLA line. I do not like giving away six-tenths of an hour, but 3.9 hours is still inside the <=4 hour target and the 92.1% closure rate is real progress.
periods.recommendations: Hold the green by pre-scheduling holiday desk coverage before Thanksgiving, not after the first storm forecast. Keep the improved closure discipline by requiring a same-day Cityworks status update for every open ticket older than 48 hours. I recommend adding a small storm-week callback script for Bayfront and South Harbor customers so response time does not sit at 3.9 hours again unless the workload justifies it.

periods.analysis: Q1 remained green, with response time improving from 3.9 hours to 3.7 hours, while SLA closure slipped from 92.1% to 90.1%. That is still above the >=90% target, but only by one-tenth of a point, which is not a cushion I would design into a bridge or a service desk. The winter pattern was predictable: more pothole-drainage cross-referrals, meter freeze calls in the upper elevations, and several handoffs to Pipeline Renewal inspection work on cast-iron segments CI-22 and CI-31. The team answered faster, but the closeout tail got longer when tickets needed field verification instead of a desk resolution.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the faster 3.7-hour response by keeping the shared queue between Customer Service and Utility Dispatch open from 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. through March. Protect the SLA margin by creating a separate Cityworks substatus for Pipeline Renewal verification so those tickets do not drift unowned. For the next quarter, I want a weekly list of all requests older than 72 hours, grouped by crew, route, and asset ID.

periods.analysis: The service desk regained room in Q2: response time improved from 3.7 hours to 3.4 hours, and SLA closure improved from 90.1% to 91.7%. That is the movement we wanted after the thin Q1 margin, and it lines up with the new dispatcher rotation and the April training cohort on Cityworks closeout codes. Irrigation turn-on season pushed calls into the Westview and Harbor Farms pressure zones, but the team separated billing questions from true utility service requests before they hit the crew board. Green here is earned: faster first response and better closure, with no accounting trick in the denominator.
periods.recommendations: Keep the dispatcher rotation in place through the summer demand period and document the exact staffing pattern that produced 3.4 hours and 91.7%. Extend the April closeout-code training to the field foremen, especially Crews 2 and 5, so completed work is not waiting on paperwork. Add a midweek dashboard check for Westview irrigation complaints and repeat low-pressure addresses tied to PRV-7.

periods.analysis: Q3 was the best operating quarter in this run so far: response time improved from 3.4 hours to 3.3 hours, and SLA closure improved from 91.7% to 93.3%. Summer normally tests Harborview because visitors, irrigation, and construction permits all arrive at once, so this was not an easy green. The permit counter routed hydrant-meter and service-lateral questions through the new PW-CS intake tag, and that kept noise out of the emergency queue. Crews also closed more work in the field using tablets on routes B-12, M-17, and H-04, which is the kind of boring operational discipline I trust.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 3.3-hour response time by keeping the PW-CS intake tag and making it mandatory for permit-related utility calls. Extend tablet closeout use to all utility crews by the end of next quarter, with Crew Leads reviewing rejected or incomplete closeouts every Friday. Use the 93.3% SLA result as the benchmark for next summer’s staffing model, not as a reason to trim coverage.

periods.analysis: We remained green in Q4, but response time moved up from 3.3 hours to 3.9 hours and SLA closure moved down from 93.3% to 92%. That is a noticeable softening from the summer high, though both measures stayed on the right side of the targets: 3.9 hours against <=4 hours and 92% against >=90%. The first atmospheric-river week loaded the queue with catch-basin, service-line leak, and water discoloration calls, and Pipeline Renewal tie-in work near CI-31 created extra customer contacts. The operation did not fail, but the margin on response time narrowed to one-tenth of an hour, and the pipes were not impressed.
periods.recommendations: Keep the green by activating storm-mode staffing when the National Weather Service forecast shows more than 1.5 inches of rain in 24 hours, with one dispatcher assigned only to water and sewer calls. Extend proactive notifications for Pipeline Renewal tie-ins to the adjacent 300-foot customer radius so preventable calls do not enter the queue. Review every ticket over 3.5 hours in December and identify whether the delay was intake, dispatch, travel time, or field diagnosis.

periods.analysis: Q1 2026 stayed green and recovered some margin: response time improved from 3.9 hours to 3.6 hours, while SLA closure eased slightly from 92% to 91.8%. I will take the three-tenths of an hour improvement, but the two-tenths-point SLA decline says we still have a closeout discipline item to watch. The North Hill valve-exercising block and Pipeline Renewal potholing around CI-22 generated customer contacts, yet the desk kept the queue moving. Harborview is growing fast, and this quarter shows the process can absorb growth if we keep the work visible by asset, crew, and route.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 3.6-hour response by continuing the storm-mode playbook as a standing winter procedure, not a one-off. Tighten the SLA side by requiring same-shift closeout notes for all completed field visits, including no-access and customer-not-home outcomes. For Q2, track new subdivision tickets from Harbor Landing Phase 3 separately so growth-related demand does not hide inside the citywide average.

periods.analysis: Q2 2026 is marked green, but the posted values for Average Customer Service Response Time and Service Requests Closed Within SLA % are null, so quarter-over-quarter movement from 3.6 hours and 91.8% cannot be calculated from the supplied data. I am treating that as a reporting gap, not proof of performance, because a blank cell does not answer a phone or close a ticket. Operationally, the team was running the Harbor Landing Phase 3 intake split and the Pipeline Renewal customer notice map, so the same controls that supported prior green quarters were still in use. Until the final Cityworks export is loaded, the status is green with a data-quality watch item bolted to it.
periods.recommendations: Load the final Q2 Cityworks extract and publish the actual response-time and SLA values before the next scorecard review. Keep the Harbor Landing Phase 3 split queue in place and compare it against the citywide queue once the null values are replaced. Do not make staffing or budget conclusions from this quarter until the missing values are reconciled against call logs, work orders, and after-hours dispatch records.

periods.analysis: The already-posted September customer-service figures are mixed: first response is 3.9 hours against a four-hour target, while 88.6% of requests closed within SLA against a 90% target. The Maple St incident generated a concentrated ticket backlog; prompt intake did not mean prompt closure.
periods.recommendations: Keep the after-hours dispatch rotation and add a corridor-level closure breakout to the next review. Check that the cleared incident backlog translates into sustained SLA recovery before changing the published target.
